extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, especially aesthetics and teleology
extracted.subtask_description: Principled criteria and distinctions for making and teaching judgements of taste, for interpreting purposiveness in nature and art, and for using teleological reasoning in reflective judgement. Drawn from Kantian aesthetics/teleology (Critique of Judgment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste: immediate pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful pleases immediately (but only in reflective intuition, not, like morality, in its concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure in a judgement of taste is not mediated by conceptual cognition; it is an immediate affective response in reflective intuition. Contrast with moral judgements, which involve concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste: disinterestedness (pleases apart from interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful pleases apart from any interest (the morally good is indeed necessarily bound up with an interest...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine aesthetic judgement is not grounded in private desires or contingent interests; if pleasure is tied to personal advantage or desire, the judgment is merely pleasant, not beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste: free imagination harmonised with understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom of the Imagination (and therefore of the sensibility of our faculty) is represented in judging the beautiful as harmonious with the conformity to law of the Understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetical judgement depends on a play of imagination that appears free yet finds conformity with cognitive laws; successful works encourage this free-harmony rather than strict conceptual determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste: subjective universality
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective principle in judging the beautiful is represented as universal, i.e. as valid for every man, though not cognisable through any universal concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although aesthetic judgements lack determinate concepts, they make a claim to universal assent. A failure to appeal beyond private taste undermines the claim to validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is not reducible to pleasant or good (reject simple empiricism or conceptual rationalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are a priori grounds of satisfaction which can subsist along with the principle of rationalism, although they cannot be comprehended in definite concepts; thus the Object of our satisfaction is neither merely the pleasant (empiricism) nor simply the good (if judged by definite concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat beauty as identical with sensory pleasure or as a straightforward cognitive/property-based good. Aesthetic judgement requires acknowledging a priori, non-conceptual grounds of satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism vs Idealism of purposiveness (prefer idealism for aesthetic purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationalism of the principle of taste is either realism (purposiveness as actual designed purpose of nature/art) or idealism (purposive harmony as a feature relative to the needs of Judgement). Because beauty is not a property of the object in itself, the idealism of purposiveness (subjective purposiveness) is the correct basis for aesthetical judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining why things appear purposive for our taste, favour an account that locates purposiveness in the subject's reflective play (ideality) rather than positing real purposes in nature or art. Beware of treating aesthetic purposiveness as evidence of literal purposes in nature (teleological realism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as symbol of morality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beautiful is the symbol of the morally Good: it gives pleasure with a claim for the agreement of every one else and makes the mind conscious of ennoblement and an elevation above sensuous pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic experience has an affinity with moral feeling; descriptions of beautiful objects often employ moral terms (majestic, innocent, modest). Use this analogy to link taste and moral Ideas, but note differences: beauty pleases immediately and apart from interest, while moral judgement is conceptually determined and bound with interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotyposis: schematical vs symbolical intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: All intuitions given to concepts a priori are either schemata (direct a priori intuitions corresponding to Understanding-concepts) or symbols (intuitions that accord by analogy to Ideas of Reason to which no adequate sensible intuition can be given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use schemata when an a priori intuition legitimately exemplifies a concept; use symbolical intuition when only an analogous presentation can stand for a supersensible Idea (e.g., representing a state by a living body vs. a machine). Beware of treating symbolical presentations as literal schemata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of taste: manner (modus) not method (methodus)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no science of the Beautiful and the judgement of taste is not determinable by means of principles; for beautiful art there is only a manner, not a method of teaching. Masters must show pupils what and how to do; universal rules serve as reminders, not prescriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching and evaluating art should emphasize exemplars, cultivation of faculties, criticism, and encouragement of genius rather than rigid rule-following. Treating models as types to be imitated stifles originality and genuine taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaedeutic to taste: cultivation of humaniora and moral feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The propaedeutic to all beautiful art lies not in precepts but in the culture of mental powers by means of elements of knowledge called humaniora; taste is at bottom a faculty for judging the sensible illustration of moral Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing taste requires broad humanistic education and moral cultivation: sympathy, communicative capacity, and moral feeling foster the shared sense of taste. Evaluation of taste should consider the subject's moral and cultural formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement: regulative (reflective) use, not constitutive (determinant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The teleological act of judgement is rightly used problematically to bring nature under principles of observation and inquiry according to analogy with purposive causality; it belongs to the reflective and not to the determinant judgement. To treat teleology as constitutive would introduce a new kind of causality improperly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply teleological reasoning heuristically to guide inquiry and observation where mechanical causality seems insufficient, but avoid asserting that natural products are literally produced by final causes. Beware of converting teleological analogy into an ontological claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective purposiveness: formal (intellectual geometry) vs real (empirical order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical figures exhibit objective purposiveness that is intellectual and merely formal (not implying a concrete purpose); by contrast, order and regularity in empirical complexes (e.g., a garden) are real purposiveness dependent on the concept of purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate intellectual/formal purposiveness (a priori, exemplified in mathematics and intellectual constructions) from empirical/material purposiveness (which presupposes purposes and may invite teleological explanation). Use appropriate standards when praising purposive regularity in abstract vs empirical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three Ideas manifested by deduction (supersensible, subjective purposiveness, purposiveness for moral freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the deduction proceeds rightly, three Ideas manifest themselves: (1) the Idea of the supersensible in general as substrate of nature; (2) the Idea of the same as principle of the subjective purposiveness of nature for our cognitive faculty; (3) the Idea of the same as principle of the purposes of freedom and the agreement of freedom with its purposes in the moral sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three regulative Ideas to resolve antinomies and to ground claims about the relation of aesthetic, cognitive, and moral faculties. They function as guiding principles rather than empirically demonstrable constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of antinomies to cognitive faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds of antinomies grounded in three cognitive faculties—Understanding, Judgement, and Reason—leading respectively to a theoretical antinomy (Understanding), an aesthetical antinomy (Judgement), and a practical antinomy (Reason) when each demands unconditional determination of its objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that conflicts (antinomy) arise when higher faculties demand the unconditioned for conditioned objects; resolving these antinomies often requires referring judgments to a supersensible substrate or reinterpreting the faculty's proper domain (e.g., treating aesthetic antinomies via ideality of purposiveness).
